## Reproducibility

Every number in this report is computed from the scripts in `sim/` and
`analysis/`, run in order from a clean clone. Global seed `20260726`. The
dataset is fetched from OSF by `analysis/00_download.R` and pinned by SHA-256;
it is not redistributed here.

Data: Kossakowski, J. J., Groot, P. C., Haslbeck, J. M. B., Borsboom, D., &
Wichers, M. (2017). Data from 'Critical Slowing Down as a Personalized Early
Warning Signal for Depression'. *Journal of Open Psychology Data*, 5: 1.
doi:10.5334/jopd.29. CC-BY 4.0.
:::

# Motivation

Mood may behave as a dynamical system with alternative stable states. If it
does, then before a transition into depression the system should show *critical
slowing down*: as the basin of attraction flattens, recovery from perturbation
slows, and the observable signature is rising autocorrelation and rising
variance [@vandeleemput2014; @wichers2016].

The published critique is that between-subject evidence cannot establish a
within-person phenomenon [@bos2014], a point the original authors conceded.
Whether intraindividual early warning signals anticipate intraindividual
transitions remains open. It is, at bottom, a time-series question about short,
noisy, unevenly-spaced series — which is where this project sits.

This report is organised around one discipline: **no detector was ever tuned
against the real data.** Phase 0 validates the machinery on simulated data with
a planted transition and known ground truth. Only then is the real dataset
downloaded.

# What critical slowing down predicts

The model is the normal form of a fold bifurcation,

$$dx = \left(-x^3 + x + c(t)\right)dt + \sigma_p\,dW,$$

with $x$ a latent mood valence and $c$ a slow control parameter. Two stable
branches exist for $|c| < 2/(3\sqrt3) = 0.385$; lowering $c$ past $-0.385$
destroys the euthymic branch and the system drops into the depressed one.

Critical slowing down is *derived*, not assumed. The local recovery rate at a
stable point is $\lambda = -3x^{*2} + 1$, and on the euthymic branch
$x^* \to 1/\sqrt3$ as the fold is approached, so $\lambda \to 0$. The linearised
process is Ornstein–Uhlenbeck, giving

$$\text{AR}(1)\ \text{over gap } \Delta = e^{\lambda\Delta} \to 1,
\qquad \text{Var} = \frac{\sigma_p^2}{2|\lambda|} \to \infty.$$

That derivation is also the yardstick: the detectors must recover it on clean
data or they are broken.

One model time unit is calibrated to 5 hours, so that far from the bifurcation
the lag-1 autocorrelation at 90-minute spacing is ≈ 0.4, a typical ESM
"emotional inertia" value. **Every statement about days of data depends on this
anchor**, and it is not swept (`DECISIONS.md` D3).

# Simulation validation {#sec-phase0}

## The gate

![](../output/figures/01_ideal_state.png)

![](../output/figures/01_ideal_indicators.png)

On dense, noise-free data the indicators rise ahead of the transition with
Kendall's $\tau \approx 0.70$, and the empirical rolling AC1 tracks the analytic
$\lambda(c)$. On a non-tipping null the same machinery gives $\tau \approx 0.02$.
Euler–Maruyama step size was verified rather than assumed.

## The trend test is anticonservative by a factor of six

```{r thr}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    `window (days)` = p0_thr$win,
    indicator = p0_thr$indicator,
    `nominal 5% critical tau` = round(p0_thr$thr_nominal, 3),
    `actual 5% point of null` = round(p0_thr$thr_emp95, 3),
    `true size of a nominal 5% test` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * p0_thr$fpr_if_nominal),
    check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Rolling windows overlap by ~93%, so the Kendall tau computed on the indicator series is heavily autocorrelated and its nominal p-value is meaningless.")
```

**A nominally 5% test rejects `r sprintf("%.0f–%.0f%%", 100*min(p0_thr$fpr_if_nominal), 100*max(p0_thr$fpr_if_nominal))`
of the time under the null.** Every threshold in this project is calibrated by
simulation or by surrogate data; nominal p-values are used nowhere.

## Measurement error biases toward the hypothesis

An AR(1) observed with additive white noise is an ARMA(1,1), so the naive lag-1
autocorrelation is attenuated by the reliability ratio $s^2/(s^2+\sigma_m^2)$.
Because $s^2$ grows on the approach to the fold, **the attenuation shrinks along
the approach**, and the measured autocorrelation rises partly for a reason
unrelated to slowing down.

![](../output/figures/03_attenuation.png)

Decomposed on a single trajectory, an observed AC1 rise of +0.118 splits into
**+0.088 from genuine slowing** and **+0.104 from the reliability ratio
improving**. Roughly half the apparent signal is measurement error attenuating
less — a bias pointing the same way as the hypothesis being tested.

## The response scale can invent the signal, or reverse it {#sec-likert}

The largest finding in Phase 0, and it was found by chasing an anomaly: the
clinical null showed a *negative* variance trend where the latent variance
genuinely rises ~14%.

The variance of a rounded variable depends on where its mean sits between two
category boundaries. Approaching a transition the latent mean *slides*, so it
moves relative to the boundaries and drags rounding variance with it.

```{r lik}
lk <- subset(p0_lik, indicator == "variance")[c("cfg", "tau_drift", "auc")]
names(lk) <- c("response model", "tau on the null (truth: mildly positive)", "AUC")
knitr::kable(lk, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Identical dynamics throughout. Only the response scale changes.")
```

![](../output/figures/07_likert_artifact.png)

Autocorrelation indicators sit at AUC 0.72–0.76 across all four response models.
Variance ranges 0.77–0.95. **A finer scale is not the fix** — the 11-point
configuration was the worst tested.

## Modelling measurement error correctly does not help

```{r me}
knitr::kable(p0_rec[c("sigma_m", "ac1_naive", "lam_ou", "lam_ou_me", "sm_hat")],
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("sigma_m", "naive AC1",
  "lambda, fit_ou", "lambda, fit_ou_me", "sigma_m recovered"),
  caption = "Parameter recovery on a stationary OU at the real ESM sampling grid. True lambda = 0.6 per hour.")
```

`fit_ou` is catastrophic at realistic noise, returning $\lambda$ twenty times too
large: it reads white measurement noise as ultra-fast mean reversion. The
state-space version recovers both parameters far better — **and still loses on
discrimination at every noise level** (AUC 0.72 / 0.62 / 0.55 against 0.91 /
0.71 / 0.65 for `ac1_ou`). On ~450-observation windows a four-parameter Kalman
fit has enough sampling variance that the indicator series is mostly noise.
Removing the bias cost more variance than the bias was worth.

## Power

![](../output/figures/04_power_grid.png)

```{r pow}
mm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("days","ppd","miss","sigma_m"), function(v){
  a <- aggregate(p0_pw["power"], list(level = p0_pw[[v]]), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(lever = v, level = as.character(a$level), power = round(a$power, 3))
}))
knitr::kable(mm, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Mean power over the rest of the 216-cell grid.")
```

**Measurement noise is the dominant lever** — a 2.6× swing, larger than anything
the study design controls.

# Reproduction {#sec-phase1}

The dataset is a single participant with a history of major depressive disorder:
`r nrow(clean$data)` beeps over `r max(clean$data$day)` days, ~10 prompts/day
protocol at `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*nrow(clean$data)/(10*max(clean$data$day)))`
realised compliance, including a double-blind antidepressant taper.

## The transition is an interpretation

![](../output/figures/P1_scl90.png)

The weekly SCL-90 depression score does not jump. It sits at 1.0–1.6 through
phases 1–3 and rises through phase 4 to a sustained 1.8–2.5. A least-squares
changepoint puts the transition at **day `r clean$transition$changepoint`**; the
first sustained crossing of baseline mean + 2 SD puts it at
**day `r clean$transition$crossing`**. Both are carried forward.

## Nominal significance versus a surrogate null

![](../output/figures/P1_indicators.png)

```{r p1}
knitr::kable(p1_comp[c("series_var","transition_def","indicator","tau","p_boot","p_nominal")],
  digits = c(0,0,0,3,3,8), row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("series","transition","indicator","tau","p (block bootstrap)","p (nominal)"),
  caption = "Pre-transition window. Same data, two nulls.")
```

**`r sum(p1_comp$p_nominal < .05)` of `r nrow(p1_comp)` tests are significant
with nominal p-values. `r sum(p1_comp$p_boot < .05)` of `r nrow(p1_comp)` survive
a moving-block bootstrap** that preserves the local dynamics but destroys the
trend. The one survivor is one test among sixteen with no multiplicity
correction.

## An out-of-sample prediction, and the test that was needed to use it

@sec-likert predicted, in simulation and before this dataset was downloaded, that
the variance indicator is confounded by an item's position on its response
scale. In this participant:

```{r p1split}
iv <- subset(p1_item, indicator == "variance")
knitr::kable(iv[order(iv$headroom), c("item","headroom","tau","p_boot")],
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("item","categories to nearest bound","tau","p (bootstrap)"),
  caption = "Variance indicator by item, pre-transition.")
```

Mean $\tau$ is **+0.62 for items within 1.5 categories of their floor** and
**−0.07 for mid-scale items**. The autocorrelation indicators show no such split.

But the three floored items are symptom items, floored *because the person is not
yet symptomatic*. Genuine symptom emergence predicts the same correlation. So:
generate a synthetic series following each item's observed mean trajectory with
**constant latent variance** — no slowing down at all — round it to the item's
scale, and run the identical pipeline.

![](../output/figures/P1_artefact_test.png)

```{r art}
near <- p1_art$headroom < 1.5
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  group = c("within 1.5 categories of floor", "mid-scale"),
  n = c(sum(near), sum(!near)),
  `observed tau` = round(c(mean(p1_art$obs_tau[near]), mean(p1_art$obs_tau[!near])), 3),
  `artefact-only tau` = round(c(mean(p1_art$sim_tau_mean[near]), mean(p1_art$sim_tau_mean[!near])), 3),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "A constant-variance synthetic reproduces most of the observed trend.")
```

The artefact-only series reproduces
**`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*mean(p1_art$sim_tau_mean[near])/mean(p1_art$obs_tau[near]))`
of the observed variance trend** in the floored items, and for
**`r sum(p1_art$p_artefact_enough > .05)` of `r nrow(p1_art)` items** the observed
trend is not beyond what rounding alone produces.

::: {.callout-important}
The variance early-warning signal in this dataset carries no demonstrable
information beyond the item mean — and the item mean is the symptom. An early
warning that is a function of current symptom level is not an early warning.
:::

# Robustness {#sec-phase2}

Preregistered in `preregistration/PREREG_phase2_phase3.md`, committed before any
Phase 2 code existed. `r nrow(p2$spec)` specifications; none failed to compute.

![](../output/figures/P2_speccurve.png)

![](../output/figures/P2_by_dimension.png)

```{r p2j}
knitr::kable(p2$joint, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = sprintf("Registered joint test. Observed S1 = %+.3f, S2 = %.3f. 100 surrogate curves per block length, entire curve recomputed each time.", p2$S1, p2$S2))
```

## Registered predictions: three of four falsified

```{r p2pred}
sc <- p2$spec[!is.na(p2$spec$tau), ]
top <- sc[sc$tau >= quantile(sc$tau, .90), ]
rng_of <- function(v) diff(range(tapply(sc$tau, sc[[v]], median, na.rm = TRUE)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  prediction = c("P1 median positive but joint p > .05",
                 "P2 top decile is majority variance-on-floored",
                 "P3 detrending moves tau more than window width",
                 "P4 only `series` flips the median sign"),
  outcome = c("FALSIFIED", "FALSIFIED", "FALSIFIED", "SUPPORTED"),
  detail = c(sprintf("tau %+.3f, p = %.3f", p2$S1, min(p2$joint$p_S1)),
             sprintf("%.0f%% of top decile", 100*mean(top$indicator=="variance" & top$series=="floored")),
             sprintf("detrend range %.3f vs window range %.3f", rng_of("detrend"), rng_of("win")),
             "no dimension flips the sign")),
  row.names = FALSE)
```

Reported as they came out. Three of four were wrong, and the way they were wrong
is the interesting part.

**The curve is robustly positive.** Median $\tau$ = `r fmt(p2$S1)`,
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*p2$S2)` of specifications positive, and no dimension —
not one — flips the sign of the median. This is the opposite of the fragility
result I expected, and it must be reported as such.

**But window width dominates everything.** Median $\tau$ runs from
`r fmt(tapply(sc$tau, sc$win, median)[1])` at 20-day windows to
`r fmt(tapply(sc$tau, sc$win, median)[4])` at 60-day windows, a range of
`r fmt(rng_of("win"))`, while detrending moves it by `r fmt(rng_of("detrend"))` —
a factor of about thirty. Wider windows mean fewer, more overlapping windows and
a smoother indicator series, which inflates $|\tau|$ mechanically. The single
largest analyst degree of freedom is the one with the least substantive content.

::: {.callout-warning}
## What the joint test does and does not license

A moving-block bootstrap destroys *all* slow temporal structure. Beating it
establishes that slow structure exists in these series — which is not in doubt,
since the participant became depressed. It does **not** establish that the
structure is critical slowing down. Combined with @sec-phase1, where the variance
component proved indistinguishable from a rounding artefact, the honest reading
is: the curve is consistently positive, and what it is detecting is not
established to be the phenomenon of interest.
:::

# Design recommendations {#sec-phase3}

Registered rule, fixed in advance: a configuration is *usable* only if power
$\ge$ 0.80 **and** false alarm rate $\le$ 0.10.

**`r sum(p3$pw$usable)` of `r nrow(p3$pw)` configurations are usable.** (P6
supported.)

## Translating into what a clinician faces

Power and false-alarm rate are per-assessment quantities. Nobody experiences
per-assessment quantities. A $D$-day monitoring window gives $365/D$
non-overlapping assessments per patient-year, and what decides deployability is
the share of raised alarms that are real.

![](../output/figures/P3_ppv.png)

```{r p3tab}
top8 <- head(p3$pw[order(-p3$pw$power), ], 6)
knitr::kable(top8[c("resp","days","ppd","miss","sigma_m","power","fpr_drift",
                    "false_alarms_per_100py","ppv_05","ppv_20","ppv_40")],
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("response","days","prompts/day","missing","sigma_m","power",
                "false alarm rate","false alarms /100 patient-yrs",
                "PPV at 5%","PPV at 20%","PPV at 40%"),
  caption = "Best-power configurations in deployment units. PPV = share of alarms that are real, at three base rates of a genuine transition.")
```

The best configuration in the entire grid — 180 days, 6 prompts/day, continuous
responses, lowest measurement noise — reaches power 0.90 and produces
**`r round(p3$pw$false_alarms_per_100py[which.max(p3$pw$power)])` false alarms per
100 patient-years**. Of every 100 alarms it raises,
**`r round(100*p3$pw$ppv_05[which.max(p3$pw$power)])` are real** in a general
population, **`r round(100*p3$pw$ppv_40[which.max(p3$pw$power)])`** even among
remitted MDD patients tapering medication — the reproduction participant's own
situation, and the most favourable base rate considered.

To make a majority of alarms real at a 5% base rate, the false alarm rate would
need to be **`r round(p3$pw$fpr_drift[which.max(p3$pw$power)]/p3$need[1])`× better**
than anything achieved. Power is not the binding constraint; base rate is, and
no amount of statistical power moves it.

## What to do if you are designing an ESM study anyway

![](../output/figures/P3_duration_density.png)

1. **Buy duration, not density.** 180 days at 3 prompts/day outperformed 120 days
   at 10, using under half the prompts. Critical slowing down is slow; sampling a
   short approach more finely does not substitute for observing a longer one.
2. **Spend on measurement quality before sampling.** Measurement noise swings
   power by 2.6×, more than any design lever. Multi-item composites, not more
   beeps.
3. **Do not use rolling variance on coarse Likert items.** @sec-likert and
   @sec-phase1 both show it measures the mean's position between category
   boundaries. Use autocorrelation-based indicators, which are weaker on clean
   data and far more robust on real data.
4. **Fix the window width in advance and report the sweep.** It is the largest
   analyst degree of freedom in the entire space.
5. **Never use a nominal Kendall p-value.** Calibrate against surrogates.

# Limitations

**This is N = 1.** One person, one transition, one taper. A single transition in
a single individual cannot establish generality — that is precisely the Bos & De
Jonge [-@bos2014] critique, and nothing here escapes it. Every Phase 1 and
Phase 2 result describes *this participant*, and the reproduction should be read
as a case study, not as evidence about a population.

**The simulation is a caricature, not a validated model of mood.** The cubic
double-well is the normal form of a fold bifurcation, so it is generic *near a
fold* — but assuming mood has a fold assumes the conclusion of the substantive
debate. Phase 0 answers "if mood were like this, could we detect it", never "is
mood like this".

**The simulation is one-dimensional.** It cannot produce cross-correlation
between emotions, which is the third indicator in the published work. That is
the largest gap between this project and the papers it reproduces.

**Phase 0's numbers are best-case.** The control parameter moves linearly and
monotonically toward the fold — the most favourable possible case for a monotone
trend statistic. Real deterioration is not monotone, and real power is lower than
anything reported here.

**The timescale anchor is unswept.** One model time unit = 5 hours, calibrated to
an ESM autocorrelation of 0.4. Published inertia estimates span roughly 0.2–0.6,
and that anchor scales every statement about days of data.

**The clinical null cannot be placed arbitrarily close to the fold.** A system
parked near a fold escapes by noise with near-certainty over a study-length
horizon, so "deteriorating but stable just short of transition" is not a state
this model can sustain. The false-alarm rates are conditional on that
construction.

**The preregistration is not blind.** Phases 0 and 1 were run before it was
written, and it says so in its own first section. It registers the untested
question — how far the conclusion moves across analyst choices — not a blind test
of whether early warning signals are present.

**Base rates are assumed, not estimated.** The 5/20/40% annual transition rates
in @sec-phase3 are plausible ranges, not estimates from these data.

# Conclusion

The theory is not refuted here. On clean simulated data the planted signal is
real and detectable. Everything that fails, fails downstream of that: in
measurement, in inference, and in deployment arithmetic.

What the project does show is that three independent mechanisms — an
anticonservative trend test, a measurement-error bias, and a discretisation
artefact — all push toward finding critical slowing down whether or not it is
present; that in the canonical dataset the variance signal is not distinguishable
from a rounding artefact; and that even a configuration meeting a conventional
power bar would raise four false alarms for every real one in the population
where it would be deployed.

The useful contribution is not a verdict on the theory. It is a specification of
what an ESM study would have to look like for the question to be answerable at
all — and the observation that the field's standard analysis is considerably more
fragile than its published confidence suggests.
